## Loading libraries
```{r}
library(readr)
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
```
## Example: random df to see value of functions

### Setting up dataframe with random numbers
```{r}
df <- tibble(
  a = rnorm(10),
  b = rnorm(10),
  c = rnorm(10),
  d = rnorm(10)
)
head(df)
```

### Without a function: manual rescaling:
```{r}
df <- df |>
  mutate(a = (a - min(a, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(a, na.rm = TRUE) - min(a, na.rm = TRUE)))

head(df)
```
Then would have to copy & paste for each column
```{r}
df <- df |>
  mutate(
    a = (a - min(a, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(a, na.rm = TRUE) - min(a, na.rm = TRUE)),
    b = (b - min(b, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(b, na.rm = TRUE) - min(b, na.rm = TRUE)),
    c = (c - min(c, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(c, na.rm = TRUE) - min(c, na.rm = TRUE)),
    d = (d - min(d, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(d, na.rm = TRUE) - min(d, na.rm = TRUE))
  )
```

### Now, create a reusable rescaling function:
```{r}
rescale01 <- function(x) {
  value <- (x - min(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(x, na.rm = TRUE) - min(x, na.rm = TRUE))
  return(value)
}

df |>
  mutate(
    a = rescale01(a),
    b = rescale01(b),
    c = rescale01(c),
    d = rescale01(d)
  )
```

### Even better: use mutate(across(everything()))
```{r}
df |>
  mutate(across(everything(), rescale01))
```

## Example: Farenheit to Celsius

### Step 1: the conversion formula
```{r}
temp_F <- 212
temp_C <- (temp_F - 32) * 5/9
temp_C
```

### Step 2: create the function structure
```{r}
f_to_celsius <- function() {
  # code goes here
}
```

### Step 3: add the formula
```{r}
f_to_celsius <- function() {
  temp_C <- (temp_F - 32) * 5/9  #formula for converting f to c
}
```

### Step 4: add the argument(s)
```{r}
f_to_celsius <- function(temp_F) { #can be anything but needs to stay consistent to inside the function
  temp_C <- (temp_F - 32) * 5/9
}
```

### Step 5: add the return statement
```{r}
f_to_celsius <- function(temp_F) { #can be anything but needs to stay consistent to inside the function
  temp_C <- (temp_F - 32) * 5/9
  return(temp_C)
}
```

### Step 6: test
```{r}
f_to_celsius(32)
f_to_celsius(212)
```

### Writing a function that converts Celsius to Kelvin:
```{r}
c_to_kelvin <- function(temp_C) { 
  temp_kelvin <- (temp_C + 273.15)
  return(temp_kelvin)
}
```
Testing:
```{r}
c_to_kelvin(0)
c_to_kelvin(100)
```

## Turning plots into functions:

### Creating a reusable plot function with the penguin dataset
```{r}
library(palmerpenguins)
library(PNWColors)
```
```{r}
pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete") #creating color palette

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g, y = bill_length_mm, color = island)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
  theme_bw()
```
### Now, setting up the function:
```{r}
myplot <- function() {
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")
  
  ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g, y = bill_length_mm, color = island)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
    theme_bw()
}
```

Making arguments broad so the function works with any data:
```{r}
myplot <- function(data, x, y) {
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")
  
  ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y, color = island)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
    theme_bw()
}
```

Testing it:
```{r}
#myplot(data = penguins, x = body_mass_g, y = bill_length_mm)
```
Error! body_mass_g exists within the penguin dataframe, but R can’t find it in the environment. We need the **curly-curly {{}}** operator, to pass column names as arguments.

New function:
```{r}
myplot <- function(data, x, y) {
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")
  
  ggplot(data, aes(x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}, color = island)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
    theme_bw()
}
```

Testing again:
```{r}
myplot(data = penguins, x = body_mass_g, y = bill_length_mm)
```

Testing again with other variables:
```{r}
myplot(data = penguins, x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm)
```
### Can add default arguments, so users don't have to specify everything
Making penguins default dataset:
```{r}
myplot <- function(data = penguins, x, y) {
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")
  
  ggplot(data, aes(x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}, color = island)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
    theme_bw()
}
```

Now you can just call column names:
```{r}
myplot(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm)
```
### Layer onto the function
You can add ggplot layers using + just like a regular plot:
```{r}
myplot(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Flipper length (mm)")
```
## Adding control flow with if-else:

The if-else statement basic example:
```{r}
a <- 6
b <- 5

if (a > b) {
  f <- 20
} else {
  f <- 10
}

f
```

### Using if-else to make function more flexible, toggling features on/off
```{r}
myplot <- function(data = penguins, x, y, lines = TRUE) {  #default: lines ARE plotted/included
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")
  
  if (lines == TRUE) {
    ggplot(data, aes(x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}, color = island)) +
      geom_point() +
      geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
      scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
      theme_bw()
  } else {
    ggplot(data, aes(x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}, color = island)) +
      geom_point() +
      scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
      theme_bw()
  }
}
```

Test with lines (default):
```{r}
myplot(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm)
```
Test without lines:
```{r}
myplot(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm, lines = FALSE)
```
